content.comment_body: The S0 interface transmits measured data using impulses. These impulses can have a frequency lower than 1Hz and a width of 30ms. According to the [product_name] specifications, the maximum input frequency for standard digital inputs is 4Hz. Based on this, it appears that normal digital inputs can handle S0 interface pulses, but can they consistently count 30ms impulses at frequencies below 4Hz?
For full assurance, it's better to use a [product_name] model equipped with fast counter inputs.

Hello, my understanding is as follows: For frequency measurements, a 50% duty cycle is usually required. If the pulse duration is less than 50%, it changes the requirements. A 30ms pulse requires the input's ability to detect that short period. If the device is limited to 4Hz, it likely cannot detect a 30ms pulse reliably. Which [product_name] and [article_no] are you using? The DC versions offer built-in high-speed counters, with some supporting up to 5kHz depending on the model. Testing it may help clarify. The input frequency for DC versions depends on the device's cycle time, so review the manual (be sure to reference your specific [product_name] version and use the correct manual). For example, in [product_name] V8, the function block cycle is typically under 0.1ms. If you use around 400 function blocks, the total cycle time is about 40ms. So with programs under 300 function blocks, handling these pulses may work. The manual also describes how to measure cycle time. Hope this helps.

[user_name]: Unfortunately, [product_name] only provides 4 fast inputs, and its expansion modules do not provide additional fast inputs. [user_name]: My preferred model is the 12/24RCE(o). Regarding frequency definitions, if the specification lists 'frequency,' it likely refers to a 50% duty cycle signal. If a signal isn't 50/50, perhaps it doesn't technically have a 'frequency.' Possibly, [company_name] means the frequency for signals with a balanced duty cycle. For your point about 4Hz and a 30ms pulse: It depends on the internal implementation. If each input has an interrupt latch, in theory it should detect impulses down to 1 microsecond, provided they don't repeat more than once every 0.25 seconds. If inputs operate just as I/O leads, then impulses shorter than 0.25 seconds may not be detected. This specific behavior is not documented.

Hello, the minimum pulse length that a [product_name] can detect is critical for your application. This depends on input/output delays and device scan time. The manual provides examples for calculating scan time. For instance, if the scan time is 100ms, the shortest pulse detectable is approximately 101ms. That corresponds to 10Hz. If you have 10ms pulses with a period of 100ms (10Hz), the device will not capture these pulses. The scan process for a [product_name] is roughly: read inputs, run the user program, and write outputs. Note that unlike a PLC, [product_name] does not have input interrupts or pulse capture features. There may be alternative solutions, though. Can you provide more details about your application, such as frequency, minimum pulse length, and any other constraints regarding S0 pulse counting?

In summary, handling S0 pulses requires fast inputs. However, this leads to a new concern: can a fast input reliably detect every 30ms pulse, even if the scan cycle exceeds 100ms? If not, then the fast input of [product_name] may still be unable to process S0 interface signals accurately.

analysis.insight_summary: Participants are evaluating if [product_name] modules—using both standard and fast inputs—can reliably process S0 interface signals. The core issue is whether short pulses (30ms) at low frequencies (under 4Hz) might be missed due to scan cycle limitations and the absence of interrupt functions, making the actual capability unclear from documentation and technical resources.
analysis.user_expectations: The user expects that the [product_name] module will be able to consistently detect and count all S0 interface pulses, specifically those of 30ms duration and occurring at frequencies below 4Hz, supported by transparent documentation and product specifications.
